summary: Defines the SRv6 network programming framework, where an operator or application encodes a sequence of instructions in the IPv6 packet header. Each instruction is identified by a Segment Identifier in the packet and carried out by one or more network nodes, and the document defines a set of basic instructions.

plainLanguage.summary: SRv6 lets a sender place an ordered list of instructions in an IPv6 packet. Each network node that recognizes a listed segment applies its assigned behavior and forwards the packet along the path.

questions: what does the end behavior do in srv6
what does the end behavior do
subtitle: Defines IPv6 segment identifiers and behaviors for steering packets through a programmed path.

tldr.problem: Networks may need to steer packets along a chosen sequence of nodes and apply specific forwarding or service actions along that path.
tldr.mechanism: An SRv6 packet carries an ordered list of IPv6 Segment Identifiers (SIDs). Each SID selects a locally defined behavior such as forwarding to the next SID, decapsulation or policy encapsulation.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines base endpoint and headend behaviors, flavors and a registry of behavior identifiers for interoperable SRv6 operation.

today: RFC 8986 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2021. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Network Programming with SRv6
sections.content:
Segment Routing uses an ordered list of segments to steer a packet. Each segment represents an instruction associated with a location in the network. A node defines the behavior locally, from forwarding to the next segment to more complex packet processing.

RFC 8986 defines the SRv6 network-programming model and a base set of behaviors for interoperable overlays with underlay optimization. It assumes familiarity with the IPv6 Segment Routing Header specification.
sections.plainLanguage: An SRv6 packet carries an ordered list of segments that tells the network which actions to perform. Each node applies the behavior associated with the segment addressed to it.

sections.title: The SRv6 Segment Identifier
sections.content:
An SRv6 Segment Identifier (SID) is an IPv6 address. The RFC describes its parts as LOC:FUNCT:ARG: a locator, a function and optional arguments. The fields may have flexible lengths, provided their total is at most 128 bits; any remaining bits MUST be zero.

The function bits identify a local behavior, but a source cannot infer that behavior from the bits alone. The control plane advertises the SID together with its behavior codepoint. A routed SID belongs to an advertised IPv6 prefix; a non-routed SID can be reached by preceding it in the SID list with an appropriate routed SID or adjacency SID.
sections.plainLanguage: A SID is an IPv6 address with a locator, a behavior identifier and optional arguments. The network advertises the SID's behavior separately because the function bits alone do not explain what the node will do.

sections.title: Endpoint Behaviors
sections.content:
The base End behavior processes the Segment Routing Header, decreases the IPv6 Hop Limit and Segments Left, copies the next SID into the IPv6 Destination Address and forwards the packet. If the Hop Limit is 1 or less, the node sends an ICMP Time Exceeded message and discards the packet.

Other endpoint behaviors select a layer-3 adjacency or routing table, remove the outer IPv6 header and forward an IPv4, IPv6 or Ethernet payload, or bind a SID to another policy. Several decapsulation behaviors MUST appear as the last segment in an SR Policy.
sections.plainLanguage: The End behavior moves the packet to its next SID and reduces its Hop Limit. Other behaviors can send it to a selected neighbor, use a specific table, remove an outer header or apply another policy.

sections.title: PSP, USP and USD Flavors
sections.content:
Flavors modify the End, End.X and End.T behaviors, individually or in combination. A node advertises a flavored SID separately from an unflavored SID and advertises PSP only when enabled by the operator.

Penultimate Segment Pop (PSP) removes an exhausted Segment Routing Header at the penultimate segment endpoint. Ultimate Segment Pop (USP) removes the header at the final endpoint before processing the next header. Ultimate Segment Decapsulation (USD) removes the outer IPv6 header and forwards the inner IPv4 or IPv6 packet.
sections.plainLanguage: PSP removes the used segment list at the next-to-last endpoint, while USP removes it at the final endpoint. USD removes the outer IPv6 header and processes the inner IP packet.

sections.title: Headend Encapsulation Behaviors
sections.content:
A headend sends traffic into an SR Policy by adding an outer IPv6 header and a Segment Routing Header containing the policy's segment list. The outer source address is the headend's address, and the outer destination is the first SID. The headend decreases the inner IPv4 TTL or IPv6 Hop Limit.

Reduced encapsulation leaves the first SID only in the outer destination address rather than repeating it in the Segment Routing Header. The L2 variants encapsulate an Ethernet frame; the encapsulating node removes the preamble and frame check sequence, and the decapsulating node regenerates them as required.
sections.plainLanguage: The headend adds an outer IPv6 header and segment list so the packet follows an SR Policy. Reduced encapsulation omits the first SID from the list because it is already the outer destination.

sections.title: Counters, Hashing and Control-Plane Signaling
sections.content:
The RFC recommends packet and byte counters for each local SID, counting traffic processed successfully. When choosing among multiple paths or adjacencies, the hash MUST include the outer IPv6 source address, destination address and flow label.

The control-plane discussion is illustrative. IGP can advertise topological behaviors and Maximum SID Depth; BGP-LS can advertise node capabilities, locators and SIDs; BGP can signal several VPN and layer-2 behaviors. SID advertisements do not themselves determine IPv6 route reachability.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers can count successfully processed traffic per SID and use outer IPv6 fields when choosing among paths. Control-plane protocols advertise which SIDs and behaviors nodes support.

sections.title: Security and Behavior Registries
sections.content:
The RFC adds no security considerations beyond Segment Routing and the Segment Routing Header specifications. It relies on a defined trust boundary for the SR domain so external traffic cannot access internal SRv6 services. The cited SRH specification defines an HMAC option that can help detect unauthorized or modified segment lists.

IANA created a registry of 16-bit SRv6 Endpoint Behavior identifiers. These codepoints identify behaviors in control-plane protocols; they are not encoded in the SID function bits. The RFC also assigns Next Header value 143 to Ethernet.
sections.plainLanguage: SRv6 services should be limited to a defined trusted domain. Behavior numbers let control-plane protocols refer consistently to the actions associated with SIDs.

items.title: LOC
items.text: Locator that leads toward the node.

items.title: FUNCT
items.text: Identifies a local behavior bound to the SID.

items.title: ARG
items.text: Optional information used by the behavior; total SID fields are at most 128 bits.
